items.hint1: Go back to the exact words God spoke when he gave the command about this tree in Genesis 2. The question asks what the command was meant to protect man from.
items.hint2: God attached one stated consequence to the command. Being sent out of the garden was a punishment that came later, after the fruit was eaten, so it was not the reason given when the command was made.
items.hint3: Do not be pulled in by the name of the tree. Ask what God said would happen 'in the day that you eat of it', and compare that with the option that simply repeats the tree's name.
items.solution:
Answer: D. physical death

In Genesis 2:17 God warned the man that in the day he ate of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil he would surely die. Death was the penalty God named when he gave the command, so the command is read as a warning to keep man from death. The exam key takes this as physical death, although many Christian teachers also see a spiritual side to it.

How to tell: find the consequence God attached to the command when he gave it. It is death, spoken before any sin had happened.

Why not the others:
A. expulsion from Eden: this was the punishment given after they ate (Genesis 3:23), not the reason stated in the command.
B. exposure to evil: this idea comes from the tree's name, but the text does not give it as the reason for the command.
C. living forever: that belongs to the tree of life, and God later sent man out of the garden so he would not eat of it and live forever.

Exam tip: when a question asks why God gave a command, look for the consequence God himself stated when he gave it, not what happened later or what a name suggests.

items.hint1: Think of Genesis 1 and the blessing God spoke on the sixth day. Look at the word 'subdue' in the stem, not just 'multiply'.
items.hint2: More than one kind of creature was told to be fruitful and multiply, so 'multiply' alone will not decide it. Plants and the sun, moon and stars received no blessing to multiply at all.
items.hint3: Between the two living creatures left, which one was given dominion, the right to rule over the rest of creation?
items.solution:
Answer: B. man

In Genesis 1:28 God blessed the man and woman he had made in his image and said, 'Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; and have dominion' over the fish, the birds and every living thing. Subduing the earth was given to human beings as God's stewards, the ones who care for creation on his behalf.

How to tell: the stem joins two things, multiply and subdue. Sea creatures and birds were also told to multiply (Genesis 1:22), but subduing the earth and ruling over it was given to man.

Why not the others:
A. vegetation: plants were made on the third day to bear seed and fruit, but were not blessed to multiply and subdue the earth.
C. animal: some animals were blessed to multiply, but they were placed under man's rule, not told to subdue the earth.
D. heavenly bodies: the sun, moon and stars were set to give light and mark days and seasons, not to multiply.

Exam tip: when a creation question pairs two duties, check both. A creature may match one word in the stem but not the other.

items.hint1: Recall what Pharaoh's two dreams meant in Genesis 41 and what Joseph advised Pharaoh to do about it.
items.hint2: The question is about what followed from Pharaoh's dreams, not the dreams of the men Joseph met in prison.
items.hint3: The dreams warned of seven good years followed by seven years of famine. Which activity would prepare Egypt for the bad years?
items.solution:
Answer: D. storage of food

Joseph explained that Pharaoh's dreams meant seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. He advised Pharaoh to set a wise man over Egypt and gather a fifth of the harvest in the good years, keeping it in the cities (Genesis 41:33-36). This was done.

How to tell: link the meaning of the dreams (famine is coming) to the practical plan (save food now). Joseph gathered grain 'like the sand of the sea' during the years of plenty (Genesis 41:49).

Why not the others:
A. elevation of the butler: the butler was restored earlier, after Joseph interpreted the butler's own dream in prison.
B. nation wide prayer: the Bible records no national prayer as a result of the interpretation.
C. recruitment of labour: overseers were appointed to gather the grain, but the outcome the text stresses is the storing of food.

Exam tip: in Joseph questions, first check whose dream is meant: Joseph's own, the butler's and baker's, or Pharaoh's. Each one has a different outcome.

items.hint1: Think about what Joseph did after he explained Pharaoh's dreams, and what kind of thinking that needed.
items.hint2: The question asks about the quality shown by this one episode. Being friendly and easy to talk to is not what interpreting dreams and giving advice show, and neither is hard physical effort.
items.hint3: Two options remain, one about moral goodness and one about how a leader thinks. Which fits a plan made for a famine that was still seven years away?
items.solution:
Answer: C. visionary

A visionary leader sees what is coming and plans for it before it arrives. Joseph read the dreams as seven good years followed by seven years of famine, then advised Pharaoh to store grain in the good years (Genesis 41:33-36). That is foresight turned into a plan.

How to tell: ask what the action needed. Interpreting the dreams and advising Pharaoh needed Joseph to look ahead and prepare, which is what visionary means.

Why not the others:
A. hardworking: Joseph did work hard later in gathering the grain, but the interpretation and advice show foresight, not effort.
B. righteous: Joseph was upright elsewhere, for example with Potiphar's wife, but this episode is about planning for the future.
D. affable: affable means friendly and easy to approach, which the interpretation and advice do not show.

Exam tip: for 'this showed that he was' questions, match the quality to the specific action in the stem, not to the person's general character.

items.hint1: Recall Exodus 2:11-12. Look at who the Egyptian was beating and how the Bible describes that person in relation to Moses.
items.hint2: At this point God had not yet called Moses at the burning bush, so the act was not done on God's command. Nothing in the story is about refusing to forgive.
items.hint3: Two options remain, one about moral uprightness and one about loyalty. Moses looked around, killed in secret and hid the body. Which quality does the Bible's phrase 'one of his people' point to?
items.solution:
Answer: C. strongly attached to his root

Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, yet when he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, 'one of his people', he killed the Egyptian (Exodus 2:11-12). The act showed that he still saw himself as a Hebrew and was loyal to his own people.

How to tell: the key words are 'his people' or 'his brethren'. The story is about whose side Moses took.

Why not the others:
A. unforgiving: the Egyptian had not wronged Moses himself, so forgiveness is not the issue.
B. upright: he killed in secret and hid the body in the sand, which the story does not present as an upright act.
D. an obedient servant of God: God had not yet called him, so he was not obeying any command.

Exam tip: when asked what an early act of a Bible leader shows, check whether it came before or after God's call. An act before the call cannot show obedience to that call.

items.hint1: This is a report brought back after Israel sent men to spy out Canaan in Numbers 13. Think about how many spies went and how they divided in their reports.
items.hint2: The twelve spies did not all agree. The Nephilim were the giants the spies described in the land, not the ones giving a report.
items.hint3: Remember what Caleb said in Numbers 13:30 and who stood with him. Then decide which side of the split this fearful statement came from.
items.solution:
Answer: C. majority of the spics

Moses sent twelve spies into Canaan. Ten came back saying, 'We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we' (Numbers 13:31). Caleb and Joshua disagreed and said Israel could take the land with God's help. ('Spics' in the options is a printing error for 'spies'.)

How to tell: 12 spies went. 10 were afraid and 2 were confident. Ten out of twelve is the majority.

Why not the others:
A. the Nephilims: they were the giants the spies said they saw, not the people who spoke.
B. all the spics: Caleb and Joshua did not share this view.
D. minority of the spics: the minority, Caleb and Joshua, gave the hopeful report.

Exam tip: in spy questions, remember the numbers 10 and 2. The ten gave the fearful report, and the two, Caleb and Joshua, trusted God.

items.hint1: Think of a time when God told Moses to pass some of his own authority to another man so that the people would obey him. Where in Moses' life does that belong?
items.hint2: Aaron was made Moses' spokesman at the burning bush, to speak for him, not to take over his authority. Handing over authority so the people will obey points to a successor.
items.hint3: Moses asked God for a man to lead the congregation so they would not be like sheep without a shepherd. Near the end of Moses' life, who was being prepared for that role?
items.solution:
Answer: C. appointment of Joshua to success Moses

Near the end of Moses' life, God told him to take Joshua, lay his hand on him before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and 'invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey' (Numbers 27:18-20). This was the public handing over of leadership from Moses to Joshua. ('Success' in the option is a printing error for 'succeed'.)

How to tell: 'your authority' means Moses' own authority as leader, and 'that the congregation may obey' shows the man would lead the people. That describes Moses' successor.

Why not the others:
A. appointment of Eleazar: Eleazar was already priest and only stood as witness at Joshua's commissioning.
B. appointment of Aaron as Moses spokesman: Aaron was to speak for Moses (Exodus 4:14-16), not to receive his authority over the people.
D. election of Eleazar to succeed Aaron: that happened on Mount Hor when Aaron's garments were put on Eleazar (Numbers 20:25-28), and these words were not spoken there.

Exam tip: when a quotation speaks of passing on authority so that 'the people may obey', look for a leader's successor, not a priest or a helper.

items.hint1: Recall God's charge to Joshua at the start of the book of Joshua, after Moses died. God tied Joshua's success to one clear practice.
items.hint2: God promised to be with Joshua as he had been with Moses, but that was a promise, not the condition. The condition was about something Joshua had to keep 'in his mouth'.
items.hint3: Joshua 1:8 speaks of doing something 'day and night' so that he would have good success. Was that about prayer, or about God's written law?
items.solution:
Answer: D. meditate upon the book of the law

God told Joshua, 'This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success' (Joshua 1:8). Success depended on knowing and obeying God's law.

How to tell: the word 'success' in the stem matches the word 'success' in Joshua 1:8, where it is joined to meditating on the law.

Why not the others:
A. follow Moses footsteps: God promised to be with Joshua as he was with Moses, but the condition he gave was the law, not copying Moses.
B. humble himself before the people: this is not part of God's charge to Joshua.
C. pray all the time: prayer is good, but it is not the condition named in Joshua 1:8.

Exam tip: when a question asks what God told someone to do 'to be successful' or 'to prosper', find the verse that uses that same word and read the condition attached to it.

items.hint1: Recall Judges 4. Barak said these words to Deborah before the battle against Sisera. Think about what Deborah was agreeing to do.
items.hint2: She was agreeing to go to war, so the answer must describe someone facing danger and guiding others. Kindness and sympathy have nothing to do with going into battle.
items.hint3: Two pairs remain: one about gentleness and patience, the other about boldness and taking charge. Which fits a woman who went with the army to fight Sisera?
items.solution:
Answer: B. courage and leadership

Barak told Deborah, 'If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go' (Judges 4:8). Deborah agreed and went with the army against Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army. Going into war shows courage, and guiding Israel's army shows leadership.

How to tell: ask what accepting the call meant in practice. It meant going to the battlefield and directing Barak, who waited for her word before he attacked (Judges 4:14).

Why not the others:
A. humility and tolerance: she agreed, but warned Barak that the glory would go to a woman, which is not about humility.
C. obedience and purity: purity has no part in the story, and the stem is about her agreeing to go to war, not about keeping a command.
D. sympathy and love: these describe kindness, not going into battle.

Exam tip: for a quality question, picture what the person actually did. Going into danger points to courage. Directing others points to leadership.

items.hint1: Read Judges 4:1-3 in your mind. The book of Judges repeats a pattern: Israel sins, God hands them to an enemy, they cry out, and God sends someone to save them.
items.hint2: The Bible does not explain the twenty years by the Canaanites' strength, and nothing in the story is about God showing love to the Canaanites.
items.hint3: Two options remain. One states God's right to use Canaan. The other states what God expects from his people. Which one explains why the harassment happened at all, given what Israel had done?
items.solution:
Answer: B. God expects obedience and faithfulness from his followers

Judges 4:1-3 says Israel 'again did what was evil in the sight of the Lord', so God sold them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, who oppressed them for twenty years. The oppression came because Israel had been unfaithful, and it teaches that God expects his people to obey him and stay faithful.

How to tell: find the cause in the text. It is Israel's sin, not Canaan's power. The lesson drawn from that cause is God's demand for obedience.

Why not the others:
A. for the Canaanites to know that God loves them: the story is about Israel's sin, not God's love for Canaan.
C. God has the right to punish by using Canaan: God did use Canaan, but this states God's power, not the reason, which was Israel's disobedience.
D. The Canaanites were stronger than the Israelites: Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots, but the text gives Israel's sin as the reason.

Exam tip: in Judges, a foreign oppression usually follows the words 'Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord'. Look for the sin as the reason and faithfulness as the lesson.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Samuel 2, where Eli warns his sons Hophni and Phinehas. The writer adds a short explanation of why they would not listen.
items.hint2: The question is not asking what their sins were, but why they would not listen to their father. The Bible gives the reason in the same verse as Eli's warning.
items.hint3: Finish 1 Samuel 2:25 in your mind. Its last clause begins with 'for'. Does that clause describe what the sons wanted, or something else?
items.solution:
Answer: D. it was the will of Lord to slay them

Eli warned his sons that sinning against the Lord was more serious than sinning against a man. The writer then says, 'But they would not listen to the voice of their father; for it was the will of the Lord to slay them' (1 Samuel 2:25). The Bible gives God's judgement as the reason.

How to tell: the reason is stated right after Eli's warning, in the clause beginning 'for'.

Why not the others:
A. they derived pleasure from their evil deeds: the text describes their sins but does not give pleasure as the reason they ignored Eli.
B. they benefited from the offerings: they did take the best of the offerings, but that was their sin, not the reason given for ignoring the warning.
C. their father's view were outmoded: nothing in the text suggests they thought Eli's views were old-fashioned.

Exam tip: when a question asks 'what was the reason', check whether the Bible states the reason in the verse itself. If it does, that stated reason is the answer, even when other options sound sensible.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Samuel 8:1-5, where the elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah. Listen to the first words they said to him.
items.hint2: This happened long after Eli had died, so any option that brings Eli into it cannot describe this request.
items.hint3: Two options remain. One repeats what the elders first said to Samuel. The other draws on a wish that comes later in the chapter. Which did the elders put first?
items.solution:
Answer: B. age of Samuel and the conduct of his sons

When Samuel grew old he made his sons judges, but they took bribes and twisted justice. The elders said to him, 'Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways; now appoint for us a king to govern us like all the nations' (1 Samuel 8:5). Samuel's old age and his sons' corruption were the reasons they gave.

How to tell: the elders named two things: 'you are old' and 'your sons do not walk in your ways'. Option B matches both.

Why not the others:
A. old age of Eli and the conduct of his sons: Eli and his sons had died long before this request.
C. failure of both Samuel and Eli to correct their sons: Eli is not part of this story, and the elders did not blame Samuel for failing to correct his sons.
D. need to fight other nations who had kings and won battles: the people did later ask for a king to fight their battles (1 Samuel 8:20), but that came after Samuel's warning, not as the reason they first gave.

Exam tip: when asked for the 'underlying' or main reason, go to the first reason the people themselves gave. Later arguments in the same chapter are often the distractors.

items.hint1: Picture the setting: Saul badly wounded in his last battle, speaking to his armour-bearer. Think of which enemy the books of Samuel call 'uncircumcised'.
items.hint2: Saul died on Mount Gilboa. His war with the Amalekites came earlier and ended in victory, so they were not the enemy closing in on him here.
items.hint3: The same word 'uncircumcised' is used for Goliath's people in David's story. Which of the remaining nations was that?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Philistines

In 1 Samuel 31:4, Saul, badly wounded by Philistine archers on Mount Gilboa, begged his armour-bearer to kill him so that 'these uncircumcised' would not come and make sport of him. Israelite men were circumcised as a sign of the covenant with God, and in Samuel the Philistines are the enemy most often called 'uncircumcised'.

How to tell: the battle on Mount Gilboa, where Saul and his sons died, was against the Philistines. David also called Goliath 'this uncircumcised Philistine' (1 Samuel 17:26).

Why not the others:
A. Ammonites: Saul defeated them at Jabesh-gilead early in his reign (1 Samuel 11), not at his death.
B. Amalekites: Saul fought them in 1 Samuel 15, the battle in which he disobeyed God, not his last battle.
C. Egyptians: Egypt was not at war with Saul.

Exam tip: in the books of Samuel, 'the uncircumcised' usually points to the Philistines. Link Saul's death to Mount Gilboa and the Philistines.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Samuel 26, when David went down to Saul's camp at night. The Bible explains why no one woke up.
items.hint2: Saul's men were an army guarding their king while they hunted David, so a wish to see David kill Saul does not fit them.
items.hint3: 1 Samuel 26:12 calls it a 'deep sleep' and says where it came from. Did it come from their own bodies, or from somewhere else?
items.solution:
Answer: D. were put to sleep by the will of the Lord

1 Samuel 26:12 says David took the spear and the jar of water from beside Saul's head, and no one saw or woke, 'for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them'. The Bible presents the sleep as God's doing, which gave David the chance to show he would not harm the Lord's anointed.

How to tell: the verse gives the cause directly: the deep sleep came from the Lord.

Why not the others:
A. were tired due to the hard day's work: the text gives no such reason.
B. wanted David to kill Saul: Saul's men were guarding him while they hunted David.
C. were afraid of heir enemies: the text says nothing about fear, and fear is more likely to keep soldiers awake than put them to sleep.

Exam tip: when a Bible event seems to happen by chance, check whether the text says the Lord caused it. Examiners often test that stated cause.

items.hint1: Recall 2 Samuel 12:15-18. Think about how David behaved while the child was sick, and why that worried his servants.
items.hint2: While the child was ill, David fasted, lay on the ground all night and would not eat, even when the elders of his house begged him. The servants' worry was about what his grief might lead to, not about his anger.
items.hint3: The servants said, 'How then can we say to him the child is dead?' Their fear was for David, not for themselves. Of the two options about David, which do their words describe?
items.solution:
Answer: D. harm himself

While the child was sick, David fasted and lay all night on the ground. When the child died, the servants said, 'He did not listen to us while the child was yet alive. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm' (2 Samuel 12:18). They feared his grief would drive him to hurt himself.

How to tell: the servants' own words end with 'he may do himself some harm'.

Why not the others:
A. go mad: the servants spoke of harm, not madness.
B. kill them: they did not fear for their own lives.
C. punish them: the child's death was not their fault, and the text shows no fear of punishment.

Exam tip: when a question asks why someone was afraid, look for the words they actually spoke in the story. The fear is often stated in their own speech.

items.hint1: Think about 1 Kings 11 and what turned Solomon's heart away from the Lord in his old age.
items.hint2: Solomon's reign was known for peace, not for leading Israel into battle. 'Contrary to the will of God' means breaking something God had commanded, not just making an unpopular choice.
items.hint3: Of the options left, which one broke a command God had already given to Israel, and led Solomon to worship other gods?
items.solution:
Answer: C. marrying many foreign wives

God had told Israel not to marry women from nations such as the Moabites, Ammonites and Sidonians, 'for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods'. Solomon married many foreign wives, and in his old age they turned his heart to other gods, so the Lord was angry with him (1 Kings 11:1-10).

How to tell: the stem says 'contrary to the will of God'. Look for the act the Bible says God had forbidden and then punished. Because of it, God said he would tear most of the kingdom from Solomon's son (1 Kings 11:11-13).

Why not the others:
A. engaging the Israelites in battle: Solomon's reign was mainly peaceful, and war is not the sin charged against him.
B. making Jeroboam take charge of labour: Solomon did put Jeroboam over the labour of the house of Joseph, but the text does not call this a sin.
D. using foreign labour for building projects: Solomon's forced labour caused bitterness among the people, but the text does not present it as breaking God's command.

Exam tip: 'contrary to the will of God' means breaking a command God gave. Separate unwise political decisions from sins the Bible says angered God.

items.hint1: These words were spoken to a new king about the heavy burden his father had placed on the people. Think of whose son was being asked, and by whom.
items.hint2: The words are about a son being asked to lighten his father's yoke, so Saul's death is not the setting. The northern tribes broke away because of the king's answer, not at the moment of this request.
items.hint3: The request was made at the gathering where the new king was to be made king. Who led the people in making it, and where did they meet?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Jeroboam, the son of Nebat led a delegation to Rehoboam

After Solomon died, Rehoboam went to Shechem, where all Israel had come to make him king. Jeroboam, who had come back from Egypt, came with the assembly of Israel and said, 'Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father' (1 Kings 12:3-4). They promised to serve Rehoboam if he did.

How to tell: 'your father' is Solomon, whose forced labour and taxes were the heavy yoke. The speakers are the people led by Jeroboam, speaking to Solomon's son Rehoboam.

Why not the others:
B. Rehoboam went to Gibeon to be installed king: the gathering was at Shechem, not Gibeon.
C. Saul was killed by the Philistines at Gibeon: Saul died on Mount Gilboa, and the words are about Solomon's yoke.
D. the Northern tribes broke away from Isreal: the break came after Rehoboam refused the request and answered harshly.

Exam tip: for 'this statement was made when' questions, put the events in order. A request comes before the refusal, and the refusal comes before the revolt.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Kings 3, where God appeared to Solomon in a dream at Gibeon and gave him wisdom. God added a promise with an 'if' attached.
items.hint2: Solomon had already offered a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon before the dream, so the condition was not about offerings. It was about how Solomon would live.
items.hint3: God pointed Solomon to the example of his father David. Which option describes a whole way of life rather than one act of worship?
items.solution:
Answer: D. walk in his ways

At Gibeon God gave Solomon wisdom, and also riches and honour he had not asked for. Then God added, 'If you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days' (1 Kings 3:14). Long life was tied to obedience.

How to tell: the promise of long days has one 'if', and it is walking in God's ways.

Why not the others:
A. offer him burnt offering: Solomon had already offered a thousand burnt offerings before the dream, and God did not make this the condition.
B. pray daily: prayer was not the condition God named.
C. sacrifice to him: sacrifice was part of worship, but God's condition was obedience in daily life.

Exam tip: when God attaches an 'if' to a promise in the Old Testament, the condition is usually obedience to his commands, not a ritual act.

items.hint1: These are mocking words. Think of the contest on Mount Carmel and whose god Elijah was making fun of.
items.hint2: Elijah mocked the god whose prophets called on him from morning until noon with no answer. Molech was the Ammonite god linked with child sacrifice, not the god in this contest.
items.hint3: Prophets of two gods were summoned to Carmel, but only one god's prophets built the altar and cried out there. Which god was that?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Baal

On Mount Carmel the 450 prophets of Baal called on Baal from morning until noon, but there was no answer. Elijah mocked them: 'Cry aloud, for he is a god; either he is musing, or he has gone aside, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened' (1 Kings 18:27). The contest showed that the Lord, not Baal, is God.

How to tell: the words 'cry aloud' and 'he is musing' belong to Elijah's taunt at Carmel, and the prophets crying aloud were Baal's.

Why not the others:
A. Ashtoreth: a goddess of the Sidonians whom Solomon followed, not the god in the Carmel contest.
B. Asherah: 400 prophets of Asherah were summoned, but the contest and the mocking were aimed at Baal.
D. Molech: the god of the Ammonites, linked with child sacrifice, and not part of Elijah's story.

Exam tip: link each false god to its story. Baal goes with Elijah, Ahab and Jezebel. Molech and Ashtoreth go with Solomon's foreign wives.

items.hint1: 'Arab' in the stem is a printing error for Ahab. Recall Elijah's first appearance in 1 Kings 17 and what he announced to Ahab.
items.hint2: Nothing in Ahab's story speaks of an earthquake or a spreading illness sent on Israel. Think instead about what Baal worshippers believed Baal controlled.
items.hint3: Baal was believed to be the god who sends rain. If God wanted to show Baal was powerless, what would he hold back from the land?
items.solution:
Answer: C. drought

Because Ahab married Jezebel and led Israel to worship Baal, Elijah told him, 'As the Lord the God of Israel lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word' (1 Kings 17:1). The drought lasted more than three years and showed that the Lord, not Baal, controls the rain.

How to tell: the punishment was aimed at Baal's claimed power. His worshippers looked to him for rain, so God withheld it.

Why not the others:
A. earthquake: no earthquake is sent as punishment in Ahab's story.
B. disease: no disease was sent on Israel for Ahab's sin.
D. pestilence: a deadly plague was not the punishment Elijah announced.

Exam tip: when a punishment comes during a clash with a false god, check what that god was believed to control. The punishment often shows the true God's power over that very thing.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Kings 21. Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard and Naboth refused to sell it. Think about what Jezebel was trying to get in the end.
items.hint2: The letters did not order an arrest or a kidnapping. They set up a fast, a false charge and a public trial, so that Naboth would be condemned by law.
items.hint3: The question asks what she 'aimed to achieve'. Separate the method written in the letters from the goal behind them, and ask which remaining option is the goal.
items.solution:
Answer: B. find justification for taking his vineyard

Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name telling the elders of Jezreel to proclaim a fast, seat Naboth in front, and bring two worthless men to accuse him of cursing God and the king, then take him out and stone him (1 Kings 21:8-10). This made Naboth's death look lawful. As soon as he was dead, she told Ahab to go and take the vineyard (1 Kings 21:15).

How to tell: separate the method from the goal. The fast, the false witnesses and the stoning were the method. The vineyard was the goal, and a trial that looked legal gave the excuse, or justification, for taking it.

Why not the others:
A. have Naboth arrested and imprisoned: the letters called for his death, not prison.
C. organize young men to stone him to death: the stoning was the means, not the aim, and the letters asked for two false witnesses, not young men.
D. have Naboth kidnapped and taken away: he was tried in public, not secretly taken.

Exam tip: when a question asks what someone 'aimed to achieve', look past the steps they took to the thing they wanted at the end.

items.hint1: These words were spoken by someone who received a letter asking him to cure a man of leprosy. Think of 2 Kings 5 and the letter Naaman carried.
items.hint2: The speaker says 'Am I God', which shows he knew he had no power to heal. A prophet would not speak like that about a healing that God later did through him.
items.hint3: The letter was written by one king and carried to another. Which king read it and tore his clothes?
items.solution:
Answer: C. King of Isreal

The king of Syria sent Naaman to the king of Israel with a letter asking him to cure Naaman of his leprosy. When the king of Israel read it, he tore his clothes and said, 'Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends word to me to cure a man of his leprosy?' (2 Kings 5:7). He feared Syria was looking for an excuse to start a quarrel.

How to tell: 'the man sends word to me' shows the speaker received the letter, and the king of Israel received it. The chapter does not give this king's name.

Why not the others:
A. Elisha: he heard of the king's fear and sent word to let Naaman come to him, so that Naaman would know there was a prophet in Israel.
B. Elijah: he is not in this story. Elisha was the prophet in Naaman's time.
D. King of Syria: he wrote the letter, so he is 'the man' who sent it, not the one complaining about it.

Exam tip: in 'who said this' questions, look for clues about the speaker inside the quotation. 'The man sends word to me' tells you the speaker received a message, not sent it.

items.hint1: Recall 2 Kings 22. Shaphan the secretary read the book of the law, found in the Temple, to King Josiah. The question asks for his very first reaction.
items.hint2: Burning the idols and removing the idolatrous priests belong to the reforms in 2 Kings 23, which came later.
items.hint3: Two options remain: a sign of personal grief, and an action sending others to ask the Lord. Which came first when Josiah heard the words?
items.solution:
Answer: C. rent his clothes

'When the king heard the words of the book of the law, he rent his clothes' (2 Kings 22:11). To rend means to tear. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief and repentance in Israel. Josiah realised that Judah had not obeyed what was written and that God's anger was great.

How to tell: follow the order in the chapter. The book is read, the king tears his clothes (verse 11), then he sends men to inquire of the Lord (verse 13). The reforms come in chapter 23.

Why not the others:
A. sent for inquiry: this came next, in verse 13, after he tore his clothes.
B. burnt all the idols: this was part of the later reforms (2 Kings 23).
D. deposed the idolatrous priest: this was also part of the later reforms (2 Kings 23:5).

Exam tip: when a question says 'first reaction' or 'immediate reaction', list the events in order and pick the earliest one. The best-known action is often a later one.

items.hint1: Recall the message the prophetess Huldah sent back to King Josiah in 2 Kings 22. She spoke first about Judah and then about Josiah himself.
items.hint2: Josiah was later killed in battle at Megiddo while still fairly young, so his reward was not a long life or victory in war.
items.hint3: Huldah said disaster would come on Jerusalem, but something would be different for Josiah because his heart was penitent. Was that about his throne, or about what his eyes would see?
items.solution:
Answer: C. not to witness Isreal’s punishment

Huldah said God would bring disaster on Jerusalem and its people for their idolatry. But because Josiah's heart was penitent and he humbled himself, tearing his clothes and weeping, God said, 'your eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place' (2 Kings 22:19-20). He was spared from seeing the punishment.

How to tell: the reward is in the second part of Huldah's message, spoken to Josiah himself. The disaster would still come, but after his death.

Why not the others:
A. given long life: Josiah died in battle at Megiddo at about thirty-nine years old (2 Kings 22:1, 23:29).
B. made victorious in battles: he was killed fighting Pharaoh Neco.
D. made king of Judah for life: he was already king, and this was not the promise Huldah gave.

Exam tip: when a question asks how God rewarded someone, look in the prophet's message for the promise that begins with 'because'. It names both the good deed and its reward.

items.hint1: Think about how the ruined walls and burnt gates made the Jews look to the nations around them. Nehemiah uses one particular word for it in chapters 1 and 2.
items.hint2: The ruins were not news of a sudden disaster, since the city had been destroyed long before. Nor were they a danger to Nehemiah, who lived far away in Susa.
items.hint3: The question asks how he saw the ruins, not what he did about them. Recall Nehemiah 2:17, where he tells the people why they should build, and match the word he used.
items.solution:
Answer: D. reproach

A reproach is a disgrace, something that brings shame on people in the eyes of others. Nehemiah heard that the survivors in Judah were 'in great affliction and reproach' because the wall was broken down (Nehemiah 1:3). Later he told the people, 'Come, let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach' (Nehemiah 2:17).

How to tell: the Bible itself uses the word reproach for the ruins, both when Nehemiah hears the news and when he calls the people to build.

Why not the others:
A. challenge: this describes how he responded, by planning and rebuilding, not the word he used for how he saw the ruins.
B. threat: the ruins were no danger to Nehemiah, who served the king in Susa.
C. surprise: Jerusalem had lain in ruins for many years, and the text describes his grief, not surprise.

Exam tip: when a question asks how a Bible character 'saw' something, look for the word the character used in the text. Separate how they saw it from what they did about it.

items.hint1: Recall 2 Kings 24 and 25, when Nebuchadnezzar's army carried the people of Judah to Babylon. Think about which people the Babylonians wanted and which they had no use for.
items.hint2: The Babylonians took away those who could lead, fight or work skilled trades, so the king's household and the fighting men were carried off.
items.hint3: Someone had to stay behind to work the land. Of the two groups left, which one does the Bible say the captain of the guard left to tend the vines and fields?
items.solution:
Answer: C. the poorest of the land

When Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, he carried away the king, his family and officials, the mighty men of valour, and the craftsmen and smiths. 'None remained, except the poorest people of the land' (2 Kings 24:14). After the city was burned, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, again 'left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and ploughmen' (2 Kings 25:12).

How to tell: the Babylonians took the people who could lead or fight, so Judah could not rebel. They left the poor to farm the land.

Why not the others:
A. all the men of valour: the fighting men were carried into exile.
B. the King's family: Jehoiachin's mother, wives and officials went to Babylon, and later Zedekiah was taken there too.
D. the old men and women: the text does not name old people as a group left behind.

Exam tip: conquerors in the Old Testament usually took the leaders, soldiers and craftsmen, and left the poor to work the land. Use that pattern for exile questions.

items.hint1: Read the stem carefully. It asks for the king's 'immediate' reaction, meaning the very first thing he did when he was told.
items.hint2: Nebuchadnezzar did not calmly invite the three men to talk things over. He was angry from the start.
items.hint3: Two options remain: the famous punishment, and his first response to the report. In Daniel 3, did he give the three men a chance to answer before the furnace?
items.solution:
Answer: D. was furious and sent for them

When the Chaldeans reported that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego would not bow to the golden image, 'Nebuchadnezzar in furious rage commanded that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought' (Daniel 3:13). He questioned them and gave them another chance to bow. Only when they refused again did he order the furnace heated seven times hotter.

How to tell: put the events in order: the report, his fury and the summons (verse 13), his questions (verses 14-15), their answer (verses 16-18), then the furnace (verses 19-20).

Why not the others:
A. invited them for discussion: he did question them, but in rage, not as a friendly invitation.
B. ordered that they be cast into fiery furnace: this came later, after they refused a second time.
C. ordered for their immediate death: he gave them another chance before ordering any punishment.

Exam tip: the word 'immediate' in a stem warns you that the best-known event is probably a later step. Put the events in order and pick the first.

items.hint1: Recall Amos 7:10-17, when Amos was prophesying at Bethel in the northern kingdom. Think about who was in charge of the sanctuary there.
items.hint2: Solomon and Rehoboam lived long before Amos. Amos prophesied in the days of Jeroboam II, not Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
items.hint3: The man who spoke these words sent a report to the king and then spoke to Amos directly. Was he the king himself, or the priest of Bethel?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Amaziah

Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reported Amos to King Jeroboam II, then told Amos, 'O seer, go, flee away to the land of Judah, and eat bread there, and prophesy there; but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary' (Amos 7:10-13). Amos replied that he was not a prophet by profession but a herdsman whom the Lord had called.

How to tell: the words 'the king's sanctuary' come from Amaziah, who served at Bethel and wanted Amos gone.

Why not the others:
A. Jeroboam: he was the king, Jeroboam II, who received Amaziah's report but does not speak to Amos in the text.
C. Rehoboam: he ruled Judah long before Amos.
D. Solomon: he died long before Amos was born.

Exam tip: when a question asks who opposed a prophet, check whether it was a king or a religious official. In Amos it was the priest Amaziah.

items.hint1: This is picture language from Amos 4, spoken against the wealthy women of Samaria who crushed the poor. Ask what it means for a person to be dragged away on a hook like a fish.
items.hint2: A hooked fish has no choice about where it goes. The picture is not about a trade the people would take up, and it says nothing about chariots.
items.hint3: Two options remain. One pictures people wandering without a leader. The other pictures people led away by a captor. Which one fits being pulled on hooks?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Isreal would be taken into exile and made slaves

Amos 4:2-3 says, 'The days are coming upon you, when they shall take you away with hooks, even the last of you with fishhooks', and the people would be cast out through the broken walls. Some ancient conquerors led captives away with hooks or rings. The picture means Israel would be dragged into exile as captives, which happened when Assyria took Samaria.

How to tell: read the image, not just the words. A hooked fish is pulled away by force, so the people would be taken away by force as captives.

Why not the others:
A. the Israelites would become fishermen in foreign lands: the hooks are used on the people, not by them.
B. the Israelites would scatter abroad like sheep without a shepherd: that is a different picture, of people lost without a leader, not captured.
C. there would be chariot to convey them to Babylon: no chariot is mentioned, and the northern kingdom's exile was to Assyria, not Babylon.

Exam tip: when a prophet uses picture language, ask what the image does to the people in it. Being hooked, bound or dragged points to captivity and exile.

items.hint1: Recall Matthew 3:13-15, when Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptised by John. Think about what John said and why.
items.hint2: Asking John for baptism was not boastful, and nothing in the story shows Jesus was afraid. The quality is about how Jesus placed himself under John.
items.hint3: John said he needed to be baptised by Jesus, not the other way round. Two options remain: one about good judgement, one about lowering oneself. Which fits the greater one asking the lesser one to baptise him?
items.solution:
Answer: C. humility

In Matthew 3:13-15 Jesus came to John to be baptised. John tried to stop him, saying, 'I need to be baptised by you, and do you come to me?' Jesus, whom the Gospels present as without sin, still asked to be baptised 'to fulfil all righteousness'. The greater one placing himself under the lesser one shows humility.

How to tell: John's own protest shows that Jesus was the greater. By insisting, Jesus chose to stand with the ordinary people who came to John to be baptised.

Why not the others:
A. arrogance: arrogance means thinking yourself above others, the opposite of what Jesus did.
B. fear: nothing in the story shows Jesus was afraid.
D. wisdom: Jesus was wise, but the request itself shows a lowly attitude rather than cleverness.

Exam tip: when a greater person chooses a lower place in a Bible story, the quality being tested is usually humility.

items.hint1: Matthew describes three temptations, each in a different place. Picture which one happened high up on the temple in Jerusalem.
items.hint2: Each place had its own challenge. The one about food was in the wilderness, and the one about worshipping the devil was on a very high mountain, so neither belongs on the temple.
items.hint3: On the temple, the devil quoted a psalm about angels catching Jesus. Was the angels' help the thing he told Jesus to do, or the promise he used to push Jesus into doing something?
items.solution:
Answer: C. throw himself down

In Matthew 4:5-6 the devil took Jesus to the pinnacle, the highest point, of the temple and said, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.' He wanted Jesus to test God by forcing a rescue, and Jesus answered from scripture, 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God.'

How to tell: match each temptation to its place.
In the wilderness: turn stones into bread.
On the pinnacle of the temple: throw yourself down.
On a very high mountain: bow down and worship.

Why not the others:
A. bow down and worship Satan: this was on the very high mountain, where the devil offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world.
B. solicit support of angels: the angels came from the psalm the devil quoted (Psalm 91:11-12) as bait, not the thing he told Jesus to do.
D. turn stone to bread: this was the first temptation, in the wilderness, after Jesus had fasted forty days.

Exam tip: for temptation questions, tie each challenge to its place: wilderness and bread, temple and jumping, mountain and worship. Luke puts the temple temptation last, so check which Gospel the question names before answering an order question.

items.hint1: Think about when Peter said these words and what had just happened in the boat.
items.hint2: Peter had just seen a huge catch of fish after a whole night of catching nothing. In the Bible, feeling suddenly sinful and unworthy is how people often react when they sense the holiness of God.
items.hint3: Peter was not reacting to Jesus as an ordinary man or as a ruler. Was he struck more by Jesus' right to give orders, or by the holy power of God at work in him?
items.solution:
Answer: B. divinity

Divinity means being God, or having the nature of God. In the Bible, people who sense God's holiness often become aware of their own sin, as Isaiah did when he cried 'Woe is me' (Isaiah 6:5). Peter's cry in Luke 5:8 is that kind of reaction, so CRS teaches it as Peter recognising Jesus' divinity.

How to tell: Peter and his partners had worked all night and caught nothing. At Jesus' word they let down the nets and caught so many fish that the nets began to break. Peter fell at Jesus' knees, called him Lord and confessed that he was sinful. A man does not confess his sin because someone is a good fisherman. He does it because he senses something holy.

Why not the others:
A. authority: Peter did obey Jesus' command, but confessing sin is a response to holiness, not to someone's right to give orders.
C. humanity: the miracle showed power beyond any ordinary human being, so it was not his humanity that Peter saw.
D. kingship: nothing in the scene is about Jesus ruling as a king.

Exam tip: when a person in the Bible suddenly feels sinful or unworthy in someone's presence, the examiner is usually pointing to a recognition of holiness or divinity. Look at the reaction, not only the words.

items.hint1: Recall what Jesus told people who wanted to follow him, such as counting the cost and taking up the cross.
items.hint2: The question asks what those demands teach. Set aside any option that has nothing to do with Jesus' teaching on following him.
items.hint3: Of the options that sound spiritual, which pair matches giving up your own comfort and pushing on without looking back?
items.solution:
Answer: B. determination and self denial

Jesus told would-be followers to deny themselves and take up their cross (Luke 9:23), to count the cost before starting (Luke 14:28-33), to put him before family, and not to look back once they had put their hand to the plough (Luke 9:62). These demands teach two lessons: self-denial, which is giving up your own wishes, and determination, which is keeping on to the end.

How to tell: match each demand to a lesson.
Taking up the cross and forsaking all: self-denial.
Counting the cost and not looking back: determination.

Why not the others:
A. education and entrepreneurship: these are about schooling and business, not about following Jesus.
C. faith and spiritual maturity: these are good Christian qualities, but they are not what the discipleship demands in these passages spell out.
D. humility and respect: these are good virtues, but the demands are about sacrifice and staying firm, not about how we treat others.

Exam tip: for discipleship questions, link the cross and forsaking all to self-denial, and the plough and counting the cost to determination. The examiner usually wants the answer that names the cost of following Jesus.

items.hint1: Recall how the parable of the unmerciful servant ends, and what the master said to the servant before handing him over.
items.hint2: Ask what changed the master's mind. He had already forgiven this servant everything, so look at what the servant did after that.
items.hint3: One option describes the servant's situation at the start of the story, and one describes what he did in the middle. Which of those made the master angry enough to jail him?
items.solution:
Answer: B. unfairly treated his fellow servant

In Matthew 18:23-35 a king forgave a servant a huge debt of ten thousand talents. That servant then seized a fellow servant who owed him only a hundred denarii and had him thrown into prison. The king called him wicked, saying, 'Should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?', and in anger handed him to the jailers. Jesus' lesson is that those whom God has forgiven must forgive others.

How to tell: the master's own words give the grounds: the servant showed no mercy to his fellow servant after receiving mercy himself. The huge debt had already been cancelled. It was brought back only because of his harshness.

Why not the others:
A. did not appreciate his master's kindness: this is close in spirit, but the master's charge names what he did to his fellow servant, not a failure to be grateful.
C. owed his lord a huge sum: this debt was forgiven at the start, and it returned only because of how he treated his fellow servant.
D. rebelled against his master: he did not rebel, he begged for patience and was forgiven.

Exam tip: when asked why someone in a parable was punished, find the master's or king's own words of judgement. They name the reason, while the rest of the story often only sets the scene.

items.hint1: Recall what Jesus taught in the Lord's Prayer, and in the verses just after it, about forgiving others.
items.hint2: Some options are rewards Jesus promised in the Beatitudes for other virtues, such as being pure in heart or making peace. Match the reward to forgiving, not to those.
items.hint3: Of the options left, one is a broad blessing and one is the same kind of thing the person gave to others. Which fits Jesus' rule that you receive as you give?
items.solution:
Answer: B. obtain pardon

Jesus taught that God's forgiveness goes together with our forgiving others: 'If you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father also will forgive you' (Matthew 6:14). In the Lord's Prayer we ask, 'Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (Matthew 6:12). Pardon means forgiveness.

How to tell: the reward matches the act. Those who forgive the debts of others are themselves forgiven by God, that is, they obtain pardon.

Why not the others:
A. be called sons of God: this is the Beatitude reward for peacemakers (Matthew 5:9).
C. receive salvation of God: this is not the promise Jesus attaches to forgiving others.
D. see God: this is the Beatitude reward for the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8).

Exam tip: learn each teaching with its matching reward. The pure in heart see God, peacemakers are called sons of God, and those who forgive are forgiven. When the options mix rewards, match the reward to the act named in the stem.

items.hint1: Recall what Jesus asked Peter, James and John to do while he went a little further on to pray.
items.hint2: In Gethsemane Jesus was about to be arrested. His charge was about the danger of that night, not about preaching or healing work.
items.hint3: Some options describe the disciples' mission at other times. Which option fits men who kept falling asleep when danger was near?
items.solution:
Answer: C. be vigilant

In the garden of Gethsemane Jesus prayed in great sorrow before his arrest. He told the disciples, 'Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak' (Matthew 26:41). To watch means to stay awake and alert, which is what vigilant means.

How to tell: Jesus came back three times and found the disciples asleep. Each time his concern was that they should keep watch, because danger and temptation were close.

Why not the others:
A. heal the sick: this was part of the mission of the twelve (Matthew 10:8), not the charge in the garden.
B. win souls for the kingdom: this belongs to the Great Commission after the resurrection, not to Gethsemane.
D. declare his wondrous deeds: this is not what Jesus asked of them in Gethsemane.

Exam tip: link each place to its charge. In Gethsemane the key words are 'watch and pray'. If an option means alert or watchful, it matches that charge.

items.hint1: Recall Jesus' trial before the high priest and the council, and who said what at each stage.
items.hint2: False witnesses brought charges first, and the high priest gave his verdict at the end. The question asks what Caiaphas himself demanded that Jesus tell them.
items.hint3: Caiaphas put Jesus under oath by the living God. Was his question about something Jesus had said, or about who Jesus was?
items.solution:
Answer: C. was the Christ

At the Jewish trial, Caiaphas the high priest said, 'I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God' (Matthew 26:63). 'Christ' means the Messiah, God's anointed one. Caiaphas wanted Jesus to answer for himself, so the council could condemn him from his own mouth.

How to tell: sort the trial into steps.
First: false witnesses spoke, and two said Jesus claimed he could destroy the temple. Jesus stayed silent.
Second: Caiaphas asked his question under oath.
Third: when Jesus answered, Caiaphas tore his robes and called it blasphemy.

Why not the others:
A. committed blasphemy: this was Caiaphas's verdict after Jesus answered, not what he asked.
B. said he would destroy the temple: this came from the false witnesses, and Jesus did not answer it.
D. instigated people against paying tax: this charge was brought before Pilate at the Roman trial (Luke 23:2).

Exam tip: in trial questions, separate the steps: what the witnesses said, what the judge asked, and what verdict followed. The verb in the stem, here 'seek to know', tells you which step is meant.

items.hint1: Recall Matthew 27:51-52, where Matthew lists the signs that happened at the moment Jesus died.
items.hint2: One of the options has a misprint: read 'was born' as 'was torn'. Matthew gives the four events in the options in a set order, and two of them, the earthquake and the splitting of the rocks, happen together.
items.hint3: The opening of the tombs is the last of these four. Of the rest, did Matthew start with something in nature or something in the house of worship?
items.solution:
Answer: B. temples curtain was born (a misprint for 'the temple curtain was torn')

Matthew 27:51-52 says that when Jesus died, 'the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom; and the earth shook, and the rocks were split; the tombs also were opened.' The curtain separated the Most Holy Place, where God's presence was, from the people. Its tearing is taught as a sign that the way to God was opened through Jesus' death.

How to tell: follow Matthew's order.
First: the temple curtain was torn in two.
Then: the earth shook and the rocks were split together.
Last of these four: the tombs were opened.

Why not the others:
A. earth shook: this happened together with the splitting of the rocks, straight after the curtain was torn.
C. tombs were opened: this came last of these four.
D. rocks split: this happened together with the earthquake, straight after the curtain was torn.

Exam tip: for 'which happened first' questions, learn the list in the Bible's own order, not by how dramatic each event seems. For Jesus' death in Matthew: the curtain was torn first, then the earth shook and the rocks split together, and then the tombs were opened.

items.hint1: Work out who is speaking, who is being spoken to, and which story of the early church in Jerusalem the words come from.
items.hint2: Peter said these words when a husband and wife kept back part of the money from land they sold. The story of Saul comes much later in Acts, and nothing about prayer happens in this scene.
items.hint3: The husband and wife were questioned separately, about three hours apart, and the words in the stem were said to the husband. What happened to him when he heard them?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Ananias immediately fell and died

In Acts 5:1-11, Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold land and kept back part of the money while pretending to give all of it to the apostles. Peter told Ananias that he had lied to the Holy Spirit, and so to God, not just to men. The story is taught as a warning about dishonesty and hypocrisy in the church.

How to tell: Acts 5:5 says, 'When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and died.' Young men then wrapped him up and buried him. About three hours later Sapphira came in, told the same lie, and also died.

Why not the others:
A. Barnabas confirmed that Saul was converted: this happened in Acts 9:27, after Saul's conversion, in a different story.
C. the apostle began to pray: Acts 5 does not say Peter prayed at this point.
D. Sapphira was buried by some young men: this happened about three hours later, after Sapphira also lied.

Exam tip: when a question quotes words and asks what happened next, first name the speaker and the person spoken to. Then pick the event that happened to that person, not to someone else in the same story.

items.hint1: Recall the problem in the Jerusalem church in Acts 6 that led the apostles to choose seven men.
items.hint2: The problem was a complaint about the daily sharing of food. Ask who complained and on whose behalf.
items.hint3: One option describes the setting at the start of Acts 6:1, and another describes the complaint itself. Which one was the actual reason the seven were chosen?
items.solution:
Answer: C. the Hellenist widows were neglected

In Acts 6:1-6 the Hellenists, Jewish believers who spoke Greek, complained against the Hebrews, the believers who spoke the local language, because the Hellenist widows were being left out in the daily sharing of food. The apostles did not want to leave preaching to serve tables, so the church chose seven men full of the Spirit and of wisdom, including Stephen and Philip, to take charge of this work.

How to tell: Acts 6:1 opens with 'when the disciples were increasing in number', which sets the scene. The same verse then gives the complaint, that the Hellenist widows were neglected, and verse 3 appoints the seven to deal with it.

Why not the others:
A. the Hebrew were very poor: the Hebrews were the side the complaint was made against, not a group in need.
B. most of the disciples were poor: the problem was unfair sharing to one group of widows, not general poverty.
D. the disciples were increasing in number: this was the background to the problem, not the problem the seven were chosen to solve.

Exam tip: when asked for the reason something was done, separate the background from the direct cause. The direct cause is the problem the action was meant to fix.

items.hint1: Recall who asked Peter this question, and what had happened at the house of Cornelius the centurion at Caesarea.
items.hint2: Peter answered by retelling his vision of the sheet full of animals, and how the Holy Spirit fell on Gentiles just as on Jewish believers. Set aside any option that says Christians should hold back from other people.
items.hint3: Of the options left, one is about how Christians should behave in front of Gentiles, and one is about how Christians should regard Gentiles. Which did Peter's defence show?
items.solution:
Answer: C. treat all men equally

In Acts 11:1-18 the circumcision party, Jewish Christians who held that believers must keep the law of circumcision, criticised Peter for eating with uncircumcised Gentiles. Peter told them of his vision, in which God said, 'What God has cleansed you must not call common', and how the Spirit fell on Cornelius's household as on the apostles at the beginning. Earlier he had said, 'God shows no partiality' (Acts 10:34). The lesson is that God accepts all people alike, so Christians should treat all people equally.

How to tell: Peter's reply ends, 'If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us, who was I that I could withstand God?' (Acts 11:17). The same gift for Jew and Gentile means equal treatment.

Why not the others:
A. not fellowship with a sinners: this is the opposite of Peter's point, since he was defending eating with Gentiles.
B. keep to their tradition: Peter was defending going beyond the Jewish custom of not eating with Gentiles.
D. live uprightly among gentiles: good conduct among Gentiles is taught elsewhere (1 Peter 2:12), but Peter's reply here was about accepting Gentiles, not about behaviour.

Exam tip: for 'what does this imply' questions, find the key sentence of the speaker's reply and ask what it teaches about people. In the Cornelius story that sentence is about God making no distinction.

items.hint1: Notice the word 'not' in the question. You are looking for the one option that was not a result of the Spirit coming at Pentecost.
items.hint2: Recall Acts 2: the apostles spoke in other tongues, Peter preached to the crowd, and about three thousand people were baptised. Check each option against these results.
items.hint3: Most of the options are things that began or grew at Pentecost. Find the one that describes the apostles' state of mind, and ask whether Pentecost produced it or took it away.
items.solution:
Answer: A. the apostles were afraid

At Pentecost (Acts 2:1-41) the Holy Spirit came on the disciples with a sound like wind and tongues like fire. Peter, who had denied Jesus out of fear about seven weeks before, stood up and preached boldly. About three thousand people accepted Jesus as the Messiah and were baptised. CRS teaches the results as the birth of the church, the beginning of evangelism and new boldness in the apostles.

How to tell: check each option against Acts 2.
The crowd accepted Jesus as Lord and Christ and was baptised.
The believers became one community, the church.
The apostles began preaching the gospel to others, which is evangelism.
Fear was not a result. The Spirit gave them boldness instead.

Why not the others:
B. the birth of the church: this is taught as a main result of Pentecost, when the first large group of believers was formed.
C. Jesus was accepted as the Mesiah: about three thousand people believed Peter's message that Jesus is Lord and Christ.
D. The beginning of evangelism: evangelism means spreading the gospel, and it began with Peter's sermon that day.

Exam tip: in a 'which is not' question, test every option against the story and pick the one that fails. Watch for an option that is the opposite of the real result, as fear is the opposite of boldness here.

items.hint1: Recall what the Lord told Ananias of Damascus about Saul, when Ananias was afraid to go to him.
items.hint2: The Lord called Saul a chosen instrument to carry his name to Gentiles, kings and the sons of Israel. That is the spreading of the faith the stem already mentions. The Lord then added a second purpose.
items.hint3: The Lord's words continue past 'to carry my name'. Recall what the rest of Acts 9:15-16 says would happen to Saul himself, and choose the option that matches it.
items.solution:
Answer: B. show him how much he must suffer for Jesus

In Acts 9:15-16 the Lord told Ananias, 'He is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel; for I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.' So Saul was called both to spread the faith and to suffer for Jesus.

How to tell: the Lord's words have two parts. The first, carrying Christ's name, is the propagation the stem already gives. The second, suffering for his name, is the other reason the question asks for.

Why not the others:
A. cast out demons in the name of Jesus: Paul did this later, for example at Philippi (Acts 16:18), but it is not given as a reason for his call.
C. encourage those who call on the name of Jesus: Saul had come to Damascus to arrest those who called on that name (Acts 9:14), and the Lord's words do not mention encouraging them.
D. lead the fight against the spread of Judaism: Saul was himself a Jew, and his call was to preach Christ, not to fight Judaism.

Exam tip: when a stem says 'besides' one reason, it has already given you half of a verse. Recall the whole verse and pick its other half.

items.hint1: Recall James 2, where James warns Christians against favouring the rich over the poor in church, and what he calls the 'royal law'.
items.hint2: James quotes the royal law from the Old Testament, and it is a command about how to treat the people around you. Set aside any option that has nothing to do with that.
items.hint3: Two options are about love for others. Which one fits a law that James sets against showing favour among fellow believers in the same church?
items.solution:
Answer: D. be each other's keeper

James 2:8 says, 'If you really fulfil the royal law, according to the scripture, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, you do well.' It is often explained as royal because it is the highest law, the law of the King. In CRS, loving your neighbour as yourself is summed up as being each other's keeper: caring for one another and treating everyone alike, rich or poor.

How to tell: James gives the royal law as his answer to partiality, where a rich man is given a good seat and a poor man is told to stand (James 2:1-9). Loving your neighbour means caring for every fellow believer equally, which is being each other's keeper.

Why not the others:
A. pray for those in authority: this is Paul's teaching in 1 Timothy 2:1-2, not the royal law.
B. do good to those who hate them: this is Jesus' teaching on loving enemies (Luke 6:27), a different command from love of neighbour in James 2.
C. refrain from sinful acts: this is too general, since the royal law is a command to love, not just a rule against wrongdoing.

Exam tip: learn key titles in the epistles with their meaning. The royal law in James is 'love your neighbour as yourself', so pick the option that describes caring for one another.

items.hint1: Recall James 5, where James gives a short instruction for each situation: suffering, cheerful and sick.
items.hint2: For the sick, James says to call the elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil. For the suffering, his instruction is only a few words long.
items.hint3: Each instruction in James 5:13-14 ties a situation to one action. Which option is the action that James keeps returning to in that passage?
items.solution:
Answer: D. pray themselves

James 5:13-14 says, 'Is any one among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praise. Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him.' The sick call others to pray for them, but the suffering are told to pray for themselves.

How to tell: read the three short commands in order.
Suffering: pray.
Cheerful: sing praise.
Sick: call the elders.
The stem already gives the one for the sick, so the answer is the one for the suffering.

Why not the others:
A. fast daily: James does not mention fasting here.
B. go to church: this is not what James tells the suffering to do.
C. read the Bible: this is good practice, but it is not James's instruction in this passage.

Exam tip: when a passage gives a list of situations, each with its own command, learn them as pairs. Here: suffering and pray, cheerful and sing, sick and call the elders.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Peter 2, where Peter compares Christians to newborn babies.
items.hint2: A baby drinks milk in order to grow. Peter's reason follows the same picture: the spiritual milk helps Christians grow up into something.
items.hint3: Peter says believers should grow up 'to' something by this milk. Recall the last word of 1 Peter 2:2, and choose the option that names it.
items.solution:
Answer: A. they will have salvation

1 Peter 2:2 says, 'Like newborn babes, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up to salvation.' The spiritual milk is usually explained as God's word. Just as a baby needs milk to grow, a Christian needs the word to grow in faith towards full salvation.

How to tell: the verse gives the purpose in one clause: 'that by it you may grow up to salvation.'

Why not the others:
B. they can be loved by the Lord: God's love is not given as the purpose of craving spiritual milk.
C. the Lord will deliver them: deliverance is not mentioned in this verse.
D. the Lord will provide for them: provision is not the reason Peter gives here.

Exam tip: when the Bible uses a comparison, like babies and milk, ask what the thing in the picture does. Milk makes a baby grow, so the answer is what the Christian grows into.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Peter 5, where Peter first speaks to the elders of the church and then to the younger members.
items.hint2: Peter's word to the young begins with 'Likewise', matching what he said to the elders. It is about the young people's attitude towards those leaders.
items.hint3: Some options do not appear in the verse at all. Of the rest, one is a general Christian duty and one is about how the young relate to the elders. Which fits Peter's word here?
items.solution:
Answer: B. submit to the elders

In 1 Peter 5:1-4 Peter tells the elders to tend the flock of God willingly and eagerly, as examples, not for money or to lord it over others. In verse 5 he turns to the young: 'Likewise you that are younger be subject to the elders.' To be subject means to submit, that is, to respect and follow their leadership. Good order in the church needs both groups to do their part.

How to tell: verse 5 names the young and the elders in one sentence, then adds that all should clothe themselves with humility.

Why not the others:
A. wait for their turn: Peter says nothing about the young waiting to become leaders.
C. mount pressure on the erring elders: this is the opposite of being subject to the elders.
D. surrender to the will of God: this is a good general duty, but Peter's instruction to the young here names the elders.

Exam tip: when a question pairs two groups, such as elders and the young, look for the instruction that names the relationship between them.
